html:
New Amsterdam was the Dutch town at the southern tip of Manhattan Island, capital of the colony of New Netherland. The map's label covers the colony along the Hudson River in 1650 and 1700.

The Dutch West India Company built Fort Amsterdam there around 1625 to guard its fur trade up the Hudson, where it bought beaver pelts from the Mahican and the Mohawk. In 1626 the director Peter Minuit bought Manhattan from the local Lenape. The town grew slowly but was famously mixed, with Dutch, Walloon, English, African and Jewish residents.

Peter Stuyvesant ruled it from 1647. In 1664 an English fleet arrived and he surrendered without a fight. The town became New York, and the Treaty of Breda of 1667 confirmed the swap: the English kept it and the Dutch kept Surinam. The Dutch retook it briefly in 1673 to 1674. Under English rule it became part of British North America, but its Dutch past lives on in names such as Harlem, Brooklyn and Wall Street.
